What is Designs.ai?

Designs.ai is a creative workspace that uses AI agents for tasks such as developing a brand direction, producing visual concepts, creating storyboards and working with video, slides and audio. The tools support different parts of a project. A brand brief tells the team what the work should feel like, an image concept shows how that might look, and a storyboard explains how the message can unfold over time.

The advantage of keeping these pieces together is that you can refer back to the approved brief as you move from one output to another. A series of attractive but unrelated images can make a campaign harder to recognize. Give every piece a reason to exist and keep the parts that express the same offer consistent.

Give the brand agent a usable brief

Imagine you are helping an online bakery promote a weekend box of pastries. The first deliverable is a set of posts that explains what the box contains and when it can be ordered. The brand direction should make the bakery feel warm and approachable. You might use soft daylight, a neutral surface, a single accent color and simple text. Share approved product photos and a few notes about what the owner wants customers to notice first.

Write the non-negotiable details in the brief. Include the product name, what is actually in the box and the correct way to order. Specify the approved colors and any words the client wants to avoid. If the product photograph needs to remain unchanged, state that clearly. A precise brief makes review easier because you can compare each design choice with a decision the client has already approved.

Decide what stays the same across every piece

A campaign needs a recognizable core. Keep the main color, typography and product styling consistent. A website banner may introduce the offer with a wide product image, while a vertical social post might show the box closer to the camera. Both can look like the same campaign if they share the same visual cues. The placement and amount of text can change to suit the format.

Save the accepted direction in a short reference that anyone on the project can read. Include one example of a successful layout and a note about why it works. If you are working with a client, ask them to approve this direction while changes are still cheap. It is easier to adjust one reference than to redo a complete set of images and scenes.

Use the image agent to explore distinct concepts

Give each image concept a purpose. One version might show the bakery box in a realistic setting. A second could provide a close view of its contents, and a third could leave room for the order deadline. These alternatives answer different design questions. Producing a long sequence of nearly identical images adds review time without giving the client a meaningful choice.

Describe the subject, viewing angle, lighting and intended crop. Include the details you want the image to preserve, such as the original packaging or the number of items. Compare the result with the real product and remove anything that could mislead a buyer. A mockup can help explain an idea to the client. Use approved product photography when a listing must show the exact item being sold.

Judge the design at its final size

View the draft on a phone if it will appear in a social feed. Check whether the product is recognizable and whether the headline can be read without opening the image. Keep space around the main subject for the text and any platform controls. A layout that looks balanced on a desktop may become difficult to read when it appears between other posts.

When the idea works, prepare the exact versions you need for each placement. Keep the editable source and approved images in a project folder. Name each export for its channel and purpose, such as a homepage hero, vertical story or square post. If someone needs to update the price or date later, they should be able to identify the correct source quickly.

Turn the message into a storyboard

For the bakery launch video, start with what a customer needs to know in the first few seconds. Show the finished box, then demonstrate what is inside and finish with the order deadline. Write a brief note for each scene that explains the subject, the intended action and any words that should appear on screen. A clear storyboard lets you review the order of the message before investing time in the video.

Use the storyboard to distinguish what needs filming from what can be illustrated. A shot of the actual pastries may be essential, while a title card or a background texture can be prepared separately. Check that the same packaging, colors and product facts appear in every scene. Make the final step practical and easy to follow. For example, show where people can find the order page and how long the offer lasts.

Refine the video and audio together

Test the sequence with a rough narration or captions. If the viewer hears one point and sees an unrelated scene, revise the order or replace the shot. Keep enough time for the viewer to read the important words. Review the ending at normal playback speed. An order deadline that flashes by too quickly creates extra work for support and may frustrate someone who wants to buy.

Select music and sound effects for the mood you want the customer to feel. Keep speech easy to understand and use sound effects to support useful moments, such as opening the box or cutting to a close view. Confirm the usage rights for the music and visuals before publishing, especially for client campaigns or paid advertisements. Keep the relevant source records with the project.

Use slides and audio where they help the client

Slides can help you present the design decisions before making the final assets. Build a short presentation with the goal, visual reference, sample layouts and the order of the video scenes. Put one decision on each slide. A client can then review whether the campaign represents the product accurately and whether the look matches the brand. Save the chosen direction with the project notes.

Audio can also support projects beyond a single social video. A short voiceover might help a product demo explain how an item is used. A recorded explanation can make a slide presentation easier to follow. Check pronunciation for names and unfamiliar terms. Review the export with captions or a transcript if the audience may need to use it without sound.

A practical review checklist for freelance projects

Check the offer before reviewing the appearance. Confirm product names, prices, availability, dates and contact details with the client. Review the image separately for details that a generation tool may have altered. Check hands, packaging text, logos and familiar objects. Even a small mistake can change how a buyer interprets the image. Resolve those details while the draft is still easy to change.

Then check the placement. Try the banner next to the real page headline. Preview a vertical post in the approximate size of a phone feed. Watch the exported video with the actual captions and sound. Ask someone to describe what they think the offer is after one viewing. If they miss the main point, adjust the layout or sequence before adding more design effects.

Compare Designs.ai with tools you already use

For quick template layouts, compare Canva. If you need a stock image or a vector file to use as an ingredient in a design, explore Freepik and Vecteezy. Review the available file formats and asset licenses before you make the design depend on a particular resource.

For direct video editing, review CapCut Pro. For detailed image editing, vector design and motion production, compare Adobe Creative Cloud. If your main task is turning scripts into scenes, compare InVideo. Match the tool to the job that takes the most time. You may already have an editor that handles the final production well and only need help preparing a stronger brief and storyboard.

How to decide if the price fits your work

List the projects that you expect to complete during the subscription period. For each one, identify the outputs you are likely to create. Estimate the time you spend on the rough direction and the client review. Then test one representative project. Include the time needed to correct details and prepare final files when comparing costs. The output that reaches the client matters more than the number of versions you can produce.

If you manage several accounts, check which materials you can share in the workspace. Use public or approved references for the first test, and keep copies of work you are allowed to retain. Review export options for the format you need. A flattened preview may be enough for an approval meeting, while an editable handover may require further work in another application.

Frequently asked questions

Is Designs.ai suitable for a first campaign?

Start with one small campaign and one clear goal. Prepare a brief, pick a visual direction and make a few assets for a real destination. Use the brand and image tools to develop the direction, then review the final work on the screen your customers will use. The first project is also a chance to learn which parts you want to keep editing manually.

Can I use the generated visuals for customer work?

Check the applicable terms for the specific materials and the intended use. Review the rights in the source images, fonts and music you supply. For a client handover, document the approved files and any relevant usage conditions. If the campaign requires an exclusive logo or an exact reproduction of the product, agree on the production method with the client before committing to the deliverables.

Will the same style appear in every image?

Use the same approved references and clear descriptions across related assets. Check each result beside the accepted direction, especially when the subject, framing or output format changes. If you need exact colors or typography, apply them during the final layout review. Keep a master design file so later versions can follow the same rules without rebuilding the campaign.
